failure_summary.description: Agent answered with a word or entity already in the clue, or a longer form, instead of the bare head. 'McCormick & Company' (corporate suffix rule), 'Treaty of Paris (1815)' for a 'his' pointer (answer Napoleon), 'Transit of Venus' where the clue already says Venus.

Missing rule for title+name clues ('Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah' -> Brunei, agent said 'Sultan of Brunei') and for 'Highland version of this instrument' -> 'Bagpipes' (agent said 'Great Highland Bagpipe').
'this type of chewing gum' -> 'bubble gum'. Agent gave a passage adjective ('synthetic') instead of the named type.
'this fruit' festival answered 'strawberry'; the key is the plural crop name 'strawberries'.
'Publishing partners: ___ & Wagnalls' answered 'Funk'; the key is the full pair 'Funk & Wagnalls'.

patch.reasoning: Four edits, each aimed at a pattern seen in this batch and none repeating earlier rejected edits. (1) Pronoun pointers ('his', 'her') and bare title+person clues should resolve to the person or country, not an event or title already in the clue. (2) Qualified-variant clues ('Highland version of this instrument', 'type of chewing gum', 'passing that Venus did') should be answered with the standard named category and the clue's own qualifier dropped. (3) Fruit and crop answers should be plural, which fixes 'strawberry'. (4) The corporate-suffix rule is stated more forcefully because it was ignored, and a narrow exception covers 'partners' clues whose key is the full pair.

edits.target: - 'One of these <role/title>' ('the 14th one of these spiritual leaders') asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content: - Pronoun pointers: a clue with 'his / her / their / its' and no 'this' ('The 1815 Treaty of Paris was signed after his final defeat at Waterloo') asks for the PERSON (or group) the pronoun stands for ('Napoleon'). Never answer with the treaty, battle, work or event already named in the clue. A bare '<Title> <Full name>' clue ('Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah', 'President X', 'Prime Minister Y') asks for the country or body he led ('Brunei'), not 'Sultan of Brunei', the title or his name.

edits.target: Other clue details (diet, ingredient, cooking method) are just conditions on the generic dish.
edits.content: - Qualified-variant clues ('The Highland version of this instrument has a blowpipe, a chanter & 3 drones'; 'Rubber is an ingredient in this type of chewing gum'; 'the rare passing in front of the sun that Venus did'): the answer is the standard name of the category the clue points to, with the clue's own qualifier removed. 'Highland version of this instrument' -> 'Bagpipes' (not 'Great Highland Bagpipe'). 'The rare passing ... that Venus did' -> 'Transit' (not 'Transit of Venus'). 'This type of chewing gum' needs a NAMED type ('bubble gum'). A descriptive adjective copied from a passage ('synthetic') does not name a type, so look for the type name the passages use (a title like 'How It's Made - Bubble Gum'). Check the candidate contains no word the clue already supplies as a qualifier.

edits.target: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories ('Bananas') or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'.
edits.content: - Use the singular form for a generic single object ('Well', not 'wells'), but keep the plural for crops, commodities and mass categories or when the clue says 'these'/'ones'. A fruit, vegetable, grain, nut or flower named as the theme of a festival, harvest, market or industry ('the Oxnard festival for this fruit') takes the PLURAL ('Strawberries', 'Apples', 'Bananas'), as do plural-only things ('Bagpipes', 'Scissors').

Drop corporate suffixes ('McCormick', not 'McCormick & Company'; also drop Inc., Corp., Co., Ltd., '& Sons'), even when the passage titles print the full legal name. For 'this spice company / this airline / this brand' answer with the bare brand name. Exception: a blank inside a famous partnership ('Publishing partners: ___ & Wagnalls', 'Partners: ___ & Jerry') asks for the full pair name as a trivia key lists it ('Funk & Wagnalls'), not the single missing word.
